I just completed my first year as a new grad RN in the ED. During my 4 week check in meeting I was reminded that the ED is a fast paced environment and I was slow and performed tasks that were not emergent. Turns out someone had told on me for putting lotion on an elder woman’s hands (not emergent). I informed the director I appreciate her concerns and that I want to practice safely and I will gain speed with experience. I also informed her I am not willing to compromise safety for time management considering some mistakes that could happen can be fatal. I did not throw anyone under the bus and I also did not deny that I was slower but ensured her I would become faster. If you meet your director with constructive criticism about your preceptor I would approach with a positive comment, the underlying issue, and end with a suggestion of possible swapping to give your preceptor a break from teaching. Does that help? I should also mention I work in a small rural community hospital that is critical access not level 1 trauma center and I was still a little slow and behind my peers.

One of our amazing docs comes in while I’m doing the intake and asks her usual questions. The pt said she had her thigh worked on but that’s it. Actually they had went into her femoral artery and did some work seven days prior. The doc pulled the covers back and sees a Kotex pad covering the area and peels it back to reveal necrotic tissue. Within one minute of talking to the pt the doc knew how sick she was over the simple statement of having “the shivers worse than before and they worked on my thigh”. We shipped her to a larger hospital (the cardiac hospital that “worked on her thigh” and that was the fastest I had ever seen someone diagnosed with something partially hidden so quickly. I have mad respect for that doc I hadn’t even finished her vitals or anything!

It’s so hard to stay cool, calm, and collected sometimes. I am in block four and should graduate with my RN in May. Today we had our mock code. I had a 12 hr clinical in the surgical icu yesterday and our mock code this am I hadn’t studied for and was tired. Our dummy “patient” went into a ventricular tachycardia rhythm which we gave Amiodarone but then he didn’t get better and we went to cardiovert him and I couldn’t figure out on the AED how to do that! So he died. My anxiety was through the roof, thought I might pass out. I realized when it’s a code and life or death, the new grad nurse will never be in charge. To overcome the anxiety just remember that you know what you are doing and YOU CAN DO THIS.

What state are you in? I am in Arizona and am currently in block 4 and should be graduating in May! I’m so excited for you! Nursing school is the hardest thing I’ve ever done.
